newsitem.title: USA: Upstream oil sector maybe too lean to stay mean.
newsitem.headline: Upstream oil sector maybe too lean to stay mean.

text.p: The upstream sector of the oil industry, benefiting from high crude prices and over a decade of cost-cutting that have halved industry payrolls, may soon find it cut key muscle and bone along with the fat, according to industry analysts.

While investors have rewarded announcements of job cuts over the last few years, and though companies have clearly learned to operate more efficiently, some analysts warn "corporate anorexia" may be compromising longer-term growth.
"In our opinion, the oil companies have become obsessed with cost reductions," said Arthur Smith, head of Connecticut-based oil consultancy John S. Herold Inc.
"As a result, some oil companies have paid a significant price in terms of their future intellectual capital," Smith added.
But many companies seem unapologetic about cost-cutting initiatives, saying their efforts have made drilling for oil much cheaper than it was 10 years ago.
"The industry is obsessed with cost reductions," said Pamela Pierce, vice president for business at Houston-based oil and gasoline exploration and production firm Vastar Resources Inc.

"Vastar was, is and will be obsessed with cost reductions in recent years and in future years. Once you lose 50 pounds, you don't want to go back," Pierce told a Herold's Pacesetters Energy Conference last week.
Few doubt that for the moment, the upstream oil sector is indeed on a roll, helped by crude oil prices that have been above $20 a barrel for much of 1996.

"We will have a reasonable margin with as low an oil price as $15 a barrel," said Michael Pink, Group Managing Director of Enterprise Oil Plc, Britain's largest independent oil exploration and production company.
Enterprise is one of many companies seen to have benefited from big cutbacks and reductions in cost structures.
"There's a degree of comfort from a management point of view we haven't seen in years," said one analyst attending the Herold conference.

To be sure, much of the cutting back has put emphasis on improved technologies which has enabled the industry to find oil in areas that bloated cost structures and inadequate technologies would 15 years ago would have precluded.
"We're getting oil and gas out of rocks we wouldn't even have looked at 10 or 12 years ago," said J.C Anderson, Chief Executive of Calgary-based Anderson Exploration Ltd.
"We did away with executive parking. It doesn't seem like much, but it sure sent out a signal that we're in this together," said Vastar's Pierce.
But according to data collected by John S. Herold Inc, since 1981 oil companies have shed 750,000 workers, or over half of the entire workforce in the industry which peaked that year at 1.4 million.
"Increased profitability is fine, as long as you're replacing reserves," said Geoffrey Roberts, president of Houston-based Madison Energy Advisors Inc.
"After the momentum that was created by the cuts wears off, I wonder what will happen," Roberts added. "It's hard to find good engineers and it's hard to find good geologists."
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1620
